title: Japan household spending real YoY, May 2026
question: Statistics Bureau of Japan Family Income and Expenditure Survey, consumption expenditures for two-or-more-person households, real year-over-year percent change, May 2026, first preliminary print
resolutionSource: Statistics Bureau of Japan Family Income and Expenditure Survey monthly preliminary report
resolutionRule: Resolve to the first preliminary Statistics Bureau of Japan Family Income and Expenditure Survey monthly report table for consumption expenditures of two-or-more-person households, real year-over-year percent change, May 2026. Use the agency-published one-decimal-percent figure from the first print released on 2026-07-07; because the PDF URL is rolling, use the PDF as captured or archived at first print and ignore later revisions or annual recalculations.
drivers: Recent official real spending prints were negative through April 2026
May 2025 comparison base was high at plus 4.7 percent
April 2026 showed less weakness than March but not a clear positive run rate
Real purchasing-power pressure still limits volume growth
One-off calendar and bonus-timing effects can move the monthly household survey materially

reasoning.text: Forecast for Japan May 2026 real household spending YoY first print

The resolver is the Statistics Bureau of Japan first preliminary monthly Family Income and Expenditure Survey print for consumption expenditures of two-or-more-person households, real year-over-year change, May 2026. The target field is the consumption expenditures, two-or-more-person households, real year-over-year percent-change line in the monthly preliminary report, reported to one decimal percent.

reasoning.call: Checked the Statistics Bureau of Japan household spending data page and current monthly preliminary report for the target series and recent official prints.
reasoning.result: The April 2026 preliminary report shows real consumption expenditures for two-or-more-person households at -0.5 percent year over year in 2026-Apr, after -2.9 percent in 2026-Mar, -1.8 percent in 2026-Feb, and -1.0 percent in 2026-Jan.

reasoning.call: Read the same official monthly report table for the recent reference class of first-print real year-over-year values.
Checked the official Statistics Bureau publication schedule page for the May 2026 household spending release date.
reasoning.result: The official schedule places the May 2026 household spending first-print release on 2026-07-07; the current report page identifies the monthly preliminary report as the release vehicle and reports April 2026 at -0.5 percent.

reasoning.text: Base-rate/reference-class anchor: the latest 12 official monthly first prints average about -0.2 percent, while the latest four average about -1.6 percent. No formal ARIMA, ETS, or regression model is used here; the prior is a transparent persistence and reference-class blend suited to an auditable fast public-release forecast.

Level and momentum effects point slightly negative: the January-April 2026 run is below zero, and May must compare against May 2025's high 4.7 percent print. That high base makes a positive May 2026 year-over-year result harder even if the month-to-month level is stable.

Policy and one-off mechanisms are mixed. Wage gains and fiscal support can lift nominal outlays, but the target is real spending, so price levels subtract from the volume measure. Calendar, weather, and sample-composition noise can still produce a large positive or negative one-month print.

Counter-consideration: April's improvement from -2.9 percent to -0.5 percent could mark a real turning point if wage settlements or durable-goods purchases pulled May up. Conversely, if the high May 2025 base and food-price pressure dominate, the print could fall below -4.0 percent.

Point calculation: 50 percent weight on the 12-month mean near -0.2 percent and 50 percent on the latest-four-month mean near -1.6 percent gives about -0.9 percent, then a roughly -0.2 point high-base adjustment for the 2025-May comparison gives -1.1 percent. The 12 cited prints have sample standard deviation about 2.5 percentage points and mean absolute deviation about 2.1 points, so an 80 percent central interval of roughly plus or minus 3 points is appropriate; I use -4.0 to 2.2 percent, slightly skewed downside because the base effect is adverse.

Upside outside-the-interval scenario: real wage gains and delayed services or durable-goods spending lift the first print above 2.2 percent. Downside outside-the-interval scenario: food and utility inflation plus the high May 2025 base push real spending below -4.0 percent. Central scenario: still-negative but less severe real spending, close to April's weakness.
